overview: Blackfoot peoples have homelands on the northern Plains across today’s Canada to United States border. The confederacy includes distinct nations with related languages and histories. Its two imported outlines are broad approximations, not fixed borders or proof of one centrally ruled empire.

periods.title: Seasonal life on the Plains
periods.summary: Families moved among seasonal camps in a homeland they continued to know through stories and practice.

periods.title: Trade, epidemic disease and bison loss
periods.summary: Nineteenth-century colonial expansion and destruction of bison herds brought severe disruption.

periods.title: Treaties and enduring nations
periods.summary: Treaty relationships and colonial restrictions transformed political life; the Blackfoot nations continue.

items.text: The present Blackfoot Confederacy brings together Siksika, Kainai, northern Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni, the Blackfeet Nation in Montana. Related identity does not erase their separate governments. The international border cuts across relationships with a homeland older than either modern country.

At Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta, stone cairns mark lanes that channelled bison toward a cliff. Layers of bones below and camps nearby preserve repeated communal hunts over millennia. Success depended on coordinated people, local geography and knowledge of the animals’ movements.

The camps below the jump were places for cutting up animals and preparing food, hides and other materials. The archaeological landscape therefore records far more than the dramatic moment at the cliff: processing a large hunt meant a great deal of shared work afterward.

Blackfoot Crossing’s Siksika account describes women as owners and caretakers of tipis. The central fire, bedding, containers and utensils had their places within the shelter. A portable home still required planning, maintenance and rules about how space was used.

Buffalo-hide covers and wooden poles could travel with a family. Poles were arranged into a travois to carry possessions, first pulled by dogs and later by horses. Larger animals could carry larger loads, helping change the scale of a household’s travelling equipment.

Stones once used to hold tipi covers down can survive as rings after the shelters themselves are gone. The park’s account distinguishes those rings from later use of pegs. A circle of ordinary stones may be the trace of a room where people once slept and talked.

The Siksika account describes cooking in a rawhide-lined pit by adding heated stones to water. Heat moved from the fire into the container through the stones. The cooking vessel did not have to sit directly over a flame to make soup.

A short modern written sample is “Niitsitapi”, translated by Blackfoot Crossing as “the Real People”. This spelling comes from a Siksika cultural source using Latin letters. It identifies a living people; the painted designs on tipis are not simply an alphabet spelling the word.

Treaty 7 was negotiated at Blackfoot Crossing in 1877. The Canadian Museum of History explains that First Nations approached treaties as agreements for peace and mutual support, while Canada sought land for settlement. Oral understandings and the written document did not neatly coincide.

A silver medal now in the Canadian Museum of History was presented to a Blackfoot delegate during those negotiations. Its clasped-hands image and 1877 inscription provide a surviving object from diplomacy whose promises remain important to the nations involved.

The surviving Old Sun school building on Siksika lands served a residential-school system that separated children from family life. University of Calgary documentation records survivors’ loneliness, including children who could see home from school yet could not freely return to their families.

Old Sun became an adult-learning facility in 1971 and an independent community college in 1978. The Siksika-led college now includes Siksika Knowledge courses as well as accredited programmes. Transforming the building’s purpose has made education a means of community direction and renewal.

ending.text: The Blackfoot nations continue on both sides of the border. Loss of bison, colonial control and schooling policies caused profound harm, but no 1783 “fall” ended the people. Their own governments, cultural institutions and relationships with the land carry the history forward.
